We've seen multiple examples of why giving Meta's Muse app full disk access on a Mac is a terrible idea, and a major new privacy issue has just come to light. It turns out that Muse analyses your communications with every person in your life on an hourly basis.

Apple says it is very concerned about this development, and says in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls around the Full Disk Access feature that has been abused to enable the above…

Meta Muse app makes this urgent

Meta recently launched its Muse personal AI agent app for iPhone and Mac. Despite the obvious foolishness of giving a Meta app unrestricted access to all your data on all your Apple devices, it quickly shot to the top of the App Store.

Sure enough, the wheels came off fast. Wired reports that security researcher Karan Joshi found that Meta instructed Muse to capture all the data needed to build a complete map of all your relationships, and things haven't improved since.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be to enable it to build a dedicated page for every person in the user's life. The instructions say that this hourly procedure gathers data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, 'collaborators' and people you 'track.' […] The instructions say: 'where they live, what they do, recurring topics (move, joint saving goals).' Instructions add that the model can keep a record of 'significant dates' such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history may include background details such as 'March trip, argument that finally resolved, last week's milestone.'

Apple tightens Full Disk Access use

You might think the prompt to grant an app Full Disk Access on a Mac is self-evidently a bad idea, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy users have handed over this all-areas pass without fully realising how dangerous it is.

Apple says the feature was designed for backup apps, but developers have now used it for much more, including AI agents. The company says it plans to 'introduce additional controls' to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when they grant this permission.

Here's what Apple must and absolutely must not do

Apple says this step is 'essential,' and I entirely agree. When the existing permission request is clearly failing to communicate the seriousness of granting the permission, Apple must make sure users really understand what they're allowing.

What I'd like to see is much more explicit text urging users not to grant the permission unless they're sure they understand the consequences. Something along the following lines:

Basically, the wording can't be too strong. I'd also be in favour of a one-off confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

However, Apple must absolutely not repeat the mistake it made with Screen Recording permission in macOS Sequoia. Granting that permission is, of course, just as dangerous and deserves a strong warning, but what Apple did was force us to confirm the permission once a week, and every time we restarted.

This was widely criticised for turning macOS into Microsoft Vista, and imposing 'a subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel' on users. I think Apple already goes too far occasionally when it asks us to reconfirm permissions on iPhone. As an example, I've granted Citymapper access to my location so it can keep providing navigation in the background, so Apple, I really don't need you to check whether I still want that permission.

Yes, the strongest possible warning for Full Disk Access is appropriate, but if somebody chooses to grant it, macOS must respect that decision. Please don't force users to confirm it every week, or in any other way. Thank you.
